name: Bengali
signature: A headline (mātrā) runs along the top of most letters, as in Devanagari, but many letters hang a pointed, triangular body from it (ক ব র), and the signs ি and ে stand in front of their consonant.
combination: A consonant carries an inherent vowel, the open ô of awe (ক = kô). A vowel sign replaces it (ন + া → না = na); ি and ে are written in front of the consonant they follow in speech. The hasanta ্ deletes the vowel, and the bare consonant fuses with the next into a conjunct (স + ্ + ক → স্ক). Most letters hang from a headline that runs along the top of a word.
notes: The Bengali track's own inventory: exactly the letters, signs and digits its lessons read (30 letters, 11 signs, 10 digits), each `sound` copied from that letter's own writing-lesson romanization. It is not the whole alphabet, so `complete` is false. Stroke order is source-gated: only rows with `penLifts` and `strokeOrderSource` carry a cited order, from native writers' pen traces stored in HP Labs India's LipiTk Bangla recognizer (counts and shares only; no trace is copied). Rows without them are recognition-only: `strokeOrder: []` means NOT VERIFIED, never none. Many letters are left out on purpose: in those traces the headline is drawn first, last, partly or not at all with no majority, or the stroke count is a near tie.

strokeOrderSource.citation: HP Labs India, Lipi Toolkit, Lipi Indic Character Recognizers 4.0, Bangla recognizer, class 7 (এ, e; user manual Table 4): stored online-handwriting prototypes from native Bengali writers (MIT licence, 2012)
strokeOrderSource.variation: The recognizer stores native Bengali writers' tablet pen traces, each resampled to 60 points. 194 of the 226 stored prototypes of the independent e are one pen-down stroke. 189 of those 194 start in the upper half, inside the small curl, and all 194 turn clockwise: round the curl, over the arch and down the right side. 190 end on the left, at the top of the hook, so the base is swept from right to left. The body is written like ba: 147 open with the headline left to right, 154 finish by climbing the stem, and 189 end at the top right. The traces do not settle which way the dot is turned, so the path makes no claim about it and draws it as a short touch. strokeOrderSource.citation: HP Labs India, Lipi Toolkit, Lipi Indic Character Recognizers 4.0, Bangla recognizer, class 46 (ং, anusvar; the recognizer's unicodeMapfile_bangla.ini): stored online-handwriting prototypes from native Bengali writers (MIT licence, 2012)
strokeOrderSource.variation: The recognizer stores native Bengali writers' tablet pen traces, each resampled to 60 points. 183 of the 189 stored prototypes of the anusvar (97%) are two pen-down strokes, a ring and a tail. Whichever comes first, 138 of the 183 (75%) turn the ring counterclockwise and 166 (91%) draw the tail from its upper-left end down to the right. The order is the least settled part: 103 of the 183 (56%) draw the ring first. Ring first, counterclockwise, then the tail down to the right is the commonest form, 71 of the 183 (39%), ahead of the tail first and then a counterclockwise ring (54); 71 of the 103 ring-first writers start the ring in its upper half, so the path starts at the top. The traces are scaled to a square, so they fix the start, the order, the turning and the pen lifts, not the proportions: the path is fitted to the bundled Noto Sans Bengali outline. The underlying HP Labs data is licensed for research use only, so only counts and shares are cited here, and no trace was copied. Handwriting varies by writer.
